title: Generative models estimate higher-order plant co-occurrence patterns
summary: A generative model fitted to 5153 observed plant patches in four Spanish dryland communities estimated that conditioning on additional species often weakens positive lower-order co-occurrence associations, with species-specific exceptions. The conditional frequencies were estimated from model-generated patches, not 300000 field observations. This is a descriptive relationship in a learned distribution; it does not establish causal ecological interactions or actual succession.
ai_technology: Generative adversarial networks fitted to species-presence distributions
organization: University of Valencia; Spanish National Research Council; University of Sussex

evidence.tested: GAN models learned joint species-presence distributions from 5153 recorded vegetation patches. Generated composition abundance and soil-affinity patterns were compared with the observed data; higher-order conditional association estimates were derived from generated configurations.
evidence.unknown: The specific third- and fourth-order conditional frequencies were not independently checked in held-out field data. Generated patches and repeated model initializations are not independent field replication. Co-occurrence does not prove competition, facilitation or other mechanisms. VAE-generated succession, pioneer rankings and restoration benefits are outside this record; reconstruction accuracy is not ecological forecast accuracy.
evidence.ai_role: GANs learn the high-dimensional joint distribution of plant presence and supply conditional co-occurrence estimates that describe how associations change when additional species are present.

source_review.scope: Full primary author-deposited published PDF front, input/model Methods, conditional-association Results and Discussion, plus independent Sol ecological-scope review and fresh primary publication metadata.
